When something is indicative, it works like a clue or a signal — it points toward something and suggests it is likely true, without being an absolute, definitive proof.

Think of it this way: a detective doesn't always find a confession or a video recording of the crime. Instead, they find clues — muddy footprints, a broken lock, a suspicious receipt. Those clues don't prove the crime happened in a certain way, but they strongly suggest it. That's exactly what "indicative" means — something is a sign that points you toward a conclusion.

The word almost always appears in the structure "indicative of [something]", meaning it is a sign of that thing.
Indicative (adjective): Serving as a sign, signal, or clue that something is likely true or exists.
Understanding the Nuance: Suggesting vs. Proving

This is the most important thing to understand about "indicative." It lives in the space between a wild guess and an absolute fact.

When something is indicative of something else, it means:

  • There is meaningful evidence or a signal pointing in a direction.
  • You are reasonably justified in drawing a conclusion from it.
  • But it is not guaranteed — it still involves some degree of inference.

For example: "A high fever is indicative of an infection." This means a high fever is a strong, meaningful sign that an infection may be present. But it doesn't prove it with 100% certainty — other things can cause fevers too. A doctor would still run tests. The fever is the clue; the diagnosis is the conclusion.

This is different from saying "a fever proves an infection" (too strong) or "a fever might possibly suggest an infection" (too weak). "Indicative" sits in the confident middle ground — it's a real, meaningful signal, not a certainty, and not a vague guess.

The strength of what "indicative" suggests depends heavily on the context and what exactly is doing the indicating.

  • Some things are strongly indicative — they point very clearly toward one conclusion, even if not absolutely certain. Example: "Bloodshot eyes and slurred speech are indicative of intoxication."
  • Some things are mildly indicative — they offer a hint, but other explanations are quite possible too. Example: "Arriving late once is not necessarily indicative of a lack of punctuality."

You can pair "indicative" with words like "strongly," "clearly," "not necessarily," or "perhaps" to control exactly how powerful the signal is.

"Her tone of voice was indicative of frustration."
→ Her tone was a signal — a clue — that frustration was there. You could hear the irritation even if she didn't say "I am frustrated."

"The test results are indicative of early-stage diabetes."
→ The results point toward that diagnosis. Doctors would likely investigate further, but the signal is clear enough to take seriously.

"The long queue outside is indicative of how popular the restaurant is."
→ Seeing many people waiting is a sign — a reasonable conclusion — that the restaurant must be very well-liked.

"His refusal to answer questions was indicative of guilt."
→ Staying silent suggested guilt. It didn't prove it, but it pointed in that direction.

"Low voter turnout is indicative of public disillusionment with politics."
→ The pattern of low turnout is being read as a meaningful signal of how people feel about the political system.

Whenever you use "indicative," you are essentially saying: "This thing (A) is a sign of that thing (B)." You are drawing an inference — connecting observable evidence to an underlying reality. The word is most useful when:

  • You cannot directly see the thing you are concluding (you can't look inside someone's mind, but their behaviour is indicative of their feelings).
  • The evidence is real and meaningful, not just a coincidence or a hunch.
  • You want to be accurate — not overstating certainty, but not understating it either.

This makes "indicative" especially common in scientific reports, medical contexts, journalism, formal analysis, and anywhere careful, evidence-based thinking is valued.

"Indicative" has a second, completely separate meaning in grammar. When used as a grammatical term, the indicative mood refers to the most common verb form — the one used to state facts, describe reality, and ask straightforward questions.

Examples of the indicative mood in use:

  • "She walks to school every day." (stating a fact)
  • "He finished his homework." (describing something that happened)
  • "Are you hungry?" (asking a question about reality)

This is contrasted with other grammatical moods, such as:

  • The subjunctive mood — used for hypothetical, wished-for, or contrary-to-fact situations. "If I were a bird, I would fly." ("were" instead of "was" is a sign of the subjunctive.)
  • The imperative mood — used to give commands. "Sit down. Be quiet."

The indicative mood, in short, is the "real world" mood — it's the grammatical mode you use to talk about things as they actually are, were, or will be. This meaning is separate from the everyday meaning of "indicative" and you will only encounter it when studying grammar or linguistics.

The word "indicative" comes from the same family as "indicate," which means to point to or show something. So if something is indicative, think of it as an arrow — it points toward a conclusion. It doesn't carry you all the way there and guarantee arrival, but it aims you firmly in the right direction.

Dark circles under someone's eyes are indicative of poor sleep. The dark circles are the arrow, pointing you toward the conclusion: this person isn't sleeping well.

That arrow image — a reliable, meaningful pointer that falls just short of absolute proof — is the heart of what "indicative" means.
